title: Nearly 1.9 Lakh Cancer Cases in India Tied to Infections, Lancet Study Finds
excerpt: A Lancet study estimates infections caused nearly 1.9 lakh of India's new cancer cases in 2024, led by HPV-linked cervical cancer, highlighting the role of vaccination and screening in prevention.
body:
• A study published in The Lancet estimates that nearly 1.9 lakh of India's 15.6 lakh new cancer cases in 2024 were attributable to viral and bacterial infections — a sizable share of the country's cancer burden that is potentially preventable.
  • Human papillomavirus (HPV) is the biggest contributor, accounting for over 1 lakh cases, mostly cervical cancer, followed by H. pylori (~47,000, gastric cancer), Epstein-Barr virus (~22,000) and hepatitis B and C (~15,300 combined, liver cancer).
  • Experts say vaccination, screening and timely treatment of these infections could prevent or catch many of these cancers early — but warn that vaccination alone is not enough without adult-woman HPV screening and reliable vaccine supply.
  • Globally, infections caused about 2.3 million new cancers in 2024 — around 12% of all diagnoses — with 77% of the burden falling on low and middle-income countries.

Nearly 1.9 lakh cancer cases diagnosed in India in 2024 were linked to viral and bacterial infections, according to a study published in The Lancet — a finding that spotlights the significant role preventable infections play in the country's cancer burden.

India recorded an estimated 15,62,581 new cancer cases in 2024, with 9,08,828 deaths, according to figures cited with the study. Of the infection-attributable cases, more than 1 lakh were linked to human papillomavirus (HPV), which causes cervical cancer and can also contribute to cancers elsewhere in the body. H. pylori, a bacterial infection affecting the stomach, was associated with around 47,000 cases, mainly gastric cancer. Epstein-Barr virus accounted for roughly 22,000 cases, while chronic hepatitis B and C infections — associated with liver cancer, particularly hepatocellular carcinoma — accounted for about 10,000 and 5,300 cases respectively.

Experts say a large share of these cancers could be prevented or detected early through vaccination, screening, diagnosis and timely treatment. HPV vaccination is the key preventive measure against HPV-related cancers, while screening programs can catch precancerous changes or early-stage cancers. Similarly, identifying and treating H. pylori infection can reduce the risk of certain stomach cancers.

Context & Background

The India figures sit within a global picture: the study estimated that around 2.3 million new cancer cases worldwide in 2024 — about 12% of all cancer diagnoses — were attributable to infections. The burden is heavily skewed: low and middle-income countries accounted for roughly 77% of all infection-related cases. Eastern Asia saw the largest regional number at 990,000, driven mainly by H. pylori and hepatitis B.

Five pathogens drive most infection-linked cancers: HPV, H. pylori, hepatitis B and C viruses, and Epstein-Barr virus. HPV is a common virus spread through close contact, including sex; around 14 high-risk types can change cell DNA over time, causing cells to grow out of control. Chronic hepatitis B and C infections can quietly damage the liver for years before cancer develops.

Writing about the findings in The Conversation, Dr John La Marca and Dr Sarah Diepstraten of the Walter and Eliza Hall Institute of Medical Research in Melbourne noted that "the connection between infections and cancer is indisputable" and that "many cancers are preventable." They pointed to treating cancer-causing infections such as HIV, H. pylori and hepatitis B and C, alongside preventive measures including vaccinations, condoms and disease screening — while flagging that the availability of these programs in poorer countries remains limited, making access a major equity issue.

Impact & Analysis

The findings carry a direct message for India's public-health programs: cancer prevention is not limited to lifestyle factors, and integrating infection control into cancer strategy could move the needle on one of the country's largest disease burdens. But Indian experts caution that the tools exist more reliably on paper than in practice.

Speaking to The Indian Express, Dr Smita Joshi, senior scientist at the Prayas health group, said vaccination alone is not enough, stressing screening of adult women with an HPV test and appropriate management if positive. Dr I S Gilada, secretary general of People's Health Organisation-India, highlighted the preventive role of HPV and hepatitis B vaccination — but noted the hepatitis B vaccine, though low-cost, faces supply shortages, and pointed to gaps in linking people who test negative for hepatitis B to vaccination.

"What is also important is screening of adult women with an HPV test and appropriate management if positive for prevention of cervical cancer."

— Dr Smita Joshi, Senior Scientist, Prayas health group

Diaspora Angle

For the diaspora, the study is a reminder that cancer-prevention norms differ by geography: many countries offer HPV vaccination to adolescents and routine HPV screening to adult women as standard care, and NRIs traveling with or caring for family in India can help close the gap by encouraging both.

What's Next

The findings strengthen the case for weaving infection prevention into India's cancer-control programs: better HPV vaccination coverage, expanded screening services, reliable hepatitis B vaccine supply, and systematic H. pylori testing and treatment. Whether the evidence translates into program funding and delivery will determine how much of the 1.9-lakh annual toll can actually be avoided.
